title: Which Passing Chips Need More Testing?
gist: Chipmakers are moving from blanket re-testing and burn-in toward model-driven, targeted screening of 'marginal' chips that pass every test yet carry latent reliability risk; the article argues extra screening only pays when the added test can actually expose the suspected failure mechanism more cheaply than the field failures it prevents, and that data latency, model drift and retest ambiguity limit what current flows can catch.

insights.claim: Semiconductor test cost and test volume are rising sharply, and the challenge of screening before system-level test is growing because a late failure puts more of the supply chain's invested value at risk.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Rising test intensity is a tailwind for ATE vendors and test-analytics software providers.
insights.quote: The cost of test and the amount of test is exploding, and the ability to test before system-level test is a challenge
insights.locator: "The cost of test and the amount of test is exploding"

insights.claim: In advanced multi-die packaging, test costs are dwarfed by scrap costs, so a few seconds of targeted screening before assembly can be justified by the value of the package it protects.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Advanced packaging shifts the economics toward more upstream test spend — supportive for ATE and test-data-analytics demand.
insights.quote: test costs are dwarfed by scrap costs once you start packaging these devices together
insights.locator: Changing limits or patterns within an existing insertion

insights.claim: Field failures are the most expensive outcome in chip manufacturing, and advanced process nodes are in some respects even more sensitive to reliability failures than older ones.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Reliability risk scales with node advancement, supporting demand for reliability-screening tools at leading edge.
insights.quote: Nothing is more expensive than a field failure
insights.locator: "Nothing is more expensive than a field failure"

insights.claim: Extra screening is only worth it when the added test can expose the suspected weakness at lower cost than the failures it prevents; a method that catches more marginal devices but sharply raises false rejects, handling damage or tester occupancy may not be worth it.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Value of test-analytics offerings hinges on precision (low false-reject rate), not just recall.
insights.locator: Monitoring tester and load-board performance helps

insights.claim: The acceptable balance of test cost versus residual risk differs by market: high-volume consumer device suppliers can tolerate more residual risk than suppliers to automotive, industrial or other high-reliability applications.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Automotive/industrial chip suppliers carry structurally higher test intensity per device.
insights.locator: The calculation also varies by market

insights.claim: Device-specific models that compare a chip's internal parametric measurements with its own expected behavior can find outliers that population-based statistics miss, even when the chip passes every test limit.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Supports the in-chip monitoring / device-level analytics category (e.g., proteanTecs) over pure statistical binning.
insights.locator: Device-level models are exposing hidden outliers

insights.claim: Design-related margin limits show up consistently across a product population, whereas material-induced variability is localized, asymmetric or statistically scattered, with only a subset of devices or wafers showing accelerated drift.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Signature shape (uniform vs localized drift) is a diagnostic for root cause — useful for yield-management tool differentiation.
insights.quote: Material-induced variability behaves differently. It is often localized, asymmetric, or statistically scattered

insights.claim: Test-data screening models degrade because manufacturing data drifts with process, equipment and product changes, so models must be retrained, monitored and validated as carefully as the measurements feeding them.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: ML-for-test is a recurring-service business (retraining/monitoring), not a one-time model sale.

insights.claim: An unexplained parametric drift across test insertions on a passing chip is a warning sign that warrants extra scrutiny, but only after ruling out temperature, calibration, contact resistance or instrument-configuration differences.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Cross-insertion traceability (device ID carried across flow) is a key enabling capability for test analytics platforms.
insights.quote: An unexplained drift is not a healthy sign

insights.claim: New chip designs and architecture changes lack reliable historical baselines, making it hard for even sophisticated screening models to separate meaningful anomalies from normal variation.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Early-ramp products of new architectures carry elevated escape risk; analytics value is lowest exactly when it is most needed.
insights.locator: Establishing a reliable baseline becomes especially difficult

themes.theme: Physical inspection of latent package defects

insights.claim: Latent interconnect defects in advanced packages — partial non-wetting, micro-bump voids, delamination and warpage — may not cause immediate failure but can become unstable under thermal or mechanical stress.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Advanced packaging expands the addressable market for X-ray and acoustic inspection tools.
insights.quote: Voiding and non-wetting may weaken an interconnect without causing an immediate open

insights.claim: Correlating X-ray or acoustic inspection with electrical measurements narrows possible failure mechanisms better than either technique alone and helps engineers choose a stress condition likely to expose the weakness.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Data fusion between inspection and electrical test is a differentiation vector for tool vendors.
insights.locator: X-ray or acoustic inspection can provide physical evidence

insights.claim: Many chipmakers burn in large fractions or nearly all of their inventory, which is costly and can itself damage parts; predictive models can identify which devices can skip burn-in and concentrate stress screening on marginal ones.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Predictive burn-in could reduce burn-in equipment hours per unit — a potential headwind for burn-in capacity demand, tailwind for analytics.
insights.quote: People are burning in large fractions of their inventory, or nearly all of it, which is expensive and can cause damage by itself
insights.locator: Burn-in is a particularly tough call

insights.claim: Advantest has built cloud infrastructure that reuses data from earlier test insertions to optimize die matching inside advanced packages and to set the right limits and patterns for post-assembly test.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Advantest is positioning test as a cross-insertion data platform, not only tester hardware.
insights.quote: We have established a kind of cloud infrastructure that is fetching data from the different test insertions

insights.claim: The extra test must target the suspected failure mechanism — e.g., different voltage/temperature characterization for timing, electrical or thermal stress for interconnect, burn-in for reliability signatures — because repeating the original test adds little if it was never sensitive to the defect.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Screening ROI depends on mechanism-matched tests rather than more test time per se.
insights.locator: Failure mechanisms determine which test comes next

insights.claim: Retesting packaged devices is not cheap insurance: socket insertions carry contact wear, contamination and seating variation, so a pass after a fail is ambiguous between a bad contact and an intermittent defect.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Retest-heavy flows hide information; keeping bin history is critical for quality — relevant for socket/contactor and test-cell monitoring suppliers.
insights.quote: Every time you put that part into the socket, there’s risk involved
insights.locator: Retesting is creating its own uncertainty

insights.claim: Customers increasingly want dedicated monitoring of the whole test cell — tester resources, load board, probe card, thermal control — to catch measurement-path drift that could create marginalities.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Test-cell health monitoring is an emerging add-on revenue stream for ATE vendors.
insights.locator: Comparing results across probe pins, boards, and testers

insights.claim: Test infrastructure optimized for throughput can delay data availability — in extreme cases STDF files are not built until the end of a lot — so problems on early wafers cannot be acted on in time.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Real-time test data streaming is a product gap that ATE/analytics vendors are racing to fill.
insights.quote: In extreme cases, STDF files aren’t built until the end of a lot
insights.locator: Decision latency is limiting what screening can catch

insights.claim: Automated screening rules carry two-sided risk: ramping screening when a model flags more parts may waste capacity if the model drifted, while cutting a test that rarely finds defects may remove needed coverage; a feedback loop tying selections to outcomes is required.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Governance and closed-loop validation are prerequisites before fabs trust ML to change test flows.
insights.locator: The rules governing those actions need attention, too
